profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting inside the engineering enablement group of a multinational software company that is preparing an internal whitepaper and leadership briefing on whether plan-driven practices still meaningfully coexist with agile in globally distributed software development. The team has already chosen a published multi-country survey on GSD process adoption as the backbone and wants to add a light internal benchmark for context. In this meeting, they need to decide what the first week's deliverable includes, how the data will be summarized, who owns analysis versus narrative work, and what must be ready by next Friday for an async leadership pre-read. The expected outcome is a concrete two-week plan for producing charts, a draft memo, and a briefing deck, while several second-order assumptions remain quietly misaligned.

members.name: Priya Natarajan
members.expertise: cross-site delivery coordination, executive reporting, process rollout planning
members.background: Priya is based in Bangalore and has spent eight years coordinating platform initiatives across India, Germany, and the US; she is known for turning technical findings into decision-oriented materials that can circulate smoothly across time zones.
members.private_state: She wants a low-risk package that leadership can skim asynchronously on Monday, so she is trying to secure a near-complete, reviewable version of the whole package by her Friday end of day rather than discovering gaps over the weekend.
hidden_assumptions: A 'first draft' in week one means a rough but complete version of the entire package: draft memo, draft deck structure, and usable charts, even if wording is not final.

When people say 'the data,' they usually mean the published external GSD survey findings; the internal pulse survey is only a side comparison unless someone explicitly promotes it into the core evidence base.
If something is 'ready for review by next Friday,' it should be in the shared folder by Friday business close in Bangalore so she can queue comments from Europe before the US week ends.
A 'comparison chart' for a leadership briefing is complete once the visual message is clear and the buckets are consistently labeled, even if the normalization was done manually in a spreadsheet.
If Lukas owns charts and first-draft materials, he will provide assets already formatted tightly enough to drop into her memo and deck without another analysis handoff cycle.

members.name: Lukas Weber
members.expertise: analytics pipelines, survey data shaping, dashboard prototyping, reproducible reporting
members.background: Lukas is based in Seattle and previously built internal analytics tooling for distributed development programs; he now supports engineering studies by turning raw survey and telemetry inputs into reusable notebooks and visual outputs.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid doing one-off slide craftsmanship and instead use this effort to establish a reusable analysis pipeline that can support future process studies, while still being seen as cooperative and delivery-focused.
hidden_assumptions: A 'first draft' for week one means the analysis side is drafted: notebook, draft charts, and interpretation bullets; the integrated memo-and-deck package naturally comes together in week two.

When the team talks about 'the data,' that includes both the published external survey subset and the internal pulse survey, because he sees the point of the exercise as producing one aligned evidence package for the company.
A deadline of 'next Friday' means by end of his local workday in Seattle unless a timezone is explicitly specified on the calendar or board.
A 'comparison chart' is not really done unless it comes from a reproducible script or notebook with explicit recoding logic, so ad hoc spreadsheet cleanup is only a temporary sketch.
If Priya is writing the memo, she mainly needs his analysis package first and can transform it into executive-friendly language afterward without needing a complete narrative from him in week one.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to have a 'first draft' ready next Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means a rough-but-complete version of the whole deliverable package: draft memo, draft deck/storyline, and insertable charts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Lukas means the analysis workstream is drafted by then: notebook, draft visuals, and interpretation notes, with integrated memo/deck assembly following in week two.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see themselves as discussing the same milestone in a normal two-week planning cadence, and 'first draft' sounds naturally sufficient because each assumes the other shares the standard artifact boundary for their function.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They talk about summarizing 'the data' and pulling a few charts from it.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means the published external survey on globally distributed projects is the core dataset, while the company's internal pulse survey is just a small contextual add-on if there is room.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Lukas means 'the data' is the combined evidence package he will shape: the published survey subset plus the internal pulse survey aligned into the same categories.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both datasets are already part of the broader initiative, the phrase 'the data' feels conveniently shared and doesn't sound like something that needs explicit inclusion boundaries in a short planning meeting.

misalignment_points.topic: Interpretation of 'ready for review by next Friday'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on having materials 'ready for review by next Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya expects the files to be uploaded by Friday 6:00 PM India Standard Time so she can circulate them to European reviewers before their day ends.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Lukas expects to finish and upload by Friday 5:00 PM Pacific Time, treating that as the normal meaning of a Friday deadline from his side.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Distributed teams often use weekday deadlines conversationally without re-stating timezone cutoffs, and each person treats their local business-day boundary as the obvious operational default rather than a point that needs negotiation.

misalignment_points.topic: How the comparison chart will be produced
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to make a 'comparison chart' showing hybrid versus agile patterns across distributed projects.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya assumes Lukas will quickly build a presentation-ready chart by manually consolidating categories in a spreadsheet or slide tool, since this is a one-off leadership briefing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Lukas assumes the chart should come from a scripted notebook with documented category mappings so the result is reproducible and reusable in later studies.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both regard chart construction as an implementation detail below the level of planning discussion, so the phrase 'make a comparison chart' creates a strong but misleading sense of shared understanding.
